title: While the Oscars Buzz Lasts, Let's Talk About What Makes a Good Movie
body:
## At the Oscars, we saw an entirely different Hollywood.

Ordinary article

The 88th Academy Awards are over. Has the excitement worn off? Good. Let's calm down and take up a serious question: what makes a good movie?

Look back at the 2015 US box office. The five most successful films, or the five audiences liked best, were *Star Wars: The Force Awakens*, *Jurassic Park*, *Avengers: Age of Ultron*, *Inside Out* and *Furious 7*. That's right: four of the year's top five were sequels.

At tonight's ceremony, though, we saw an entirely different Hollywood. Best Picture went to *Spotlight*, a drama made for just US$20 million, the budget ceiling for the Independent Spirit Awards, the main prize for independent film. It has none of those blockbusters' lavish effects, none of their huge budgets, none of their flashy, crowd-pleasing plotting. It tells the story of a group of journalists. It took just US$59 million at the box office.

![The cast of Spotlight. Photo: Kevin Winter/Getty Images](/uploads/image/201602/04f3598c689f.jpg)

The film the Oscars judged the best of 2015 did unremarkable business. The gap comes down to one fact: young people drive the US box office.

The Motion Picture Association of America's market statistics show it. From 2010 to 2014, Americans aged 12 to 24 went to the movies most often, more than six times a year on average. Next came 25- to 39-year-olds, at 3.7 to 5 times a year. People under 40 are the backbone of the market: over those years they bought about 65% of all tickets and pushed a handful of blockbusters to the top of the box-office charts.

The Academy's voters, however, take little interest in what young people like. This is an old complaint. In 2012 the *Los Angeles Times* published figures that critics of the Oscars have cited ever since: the Academy then had 5,765 voters, their median age was 62, and only 14% were under 50. These "old folks" do not share young people's tastes, and they see no need to bend to new, untested standards.

Edward Jay Epstein, a veteran investigative journalist, made the same point a few years ago in his book *The Hollywood Economist*. Of the 2009 Best Picture nominees, he wrote: "What these films have in common is that they have little to do with the real business of the Hollywood studios, which is showing films aimed at teenage audiences on 3,000 or more screens around the world."

Most Oscar nominees and winners have no ambition to win over the world's teenagers. In the eyes of Hollywood's elite, Epstein wrote, these films are the equivalent of Mozart in music or avant-garde painters in art.

Dig into the question and you find that what Hollywood does today has little to do with what the Oscars reward. As our earlier Hollywood Report series argued, the core of Hollywood may now be that much-hated term, IP (intellectual property).

Take Disney, the studio everyone most "admires." This diversified, multi-brand "entertainment company" routinely calls its hit films "valuable assets." Around those assets it builds a chain of businesses long enough to stamp its products on your memory: films, television, theme parks, merchandise, games and every sort of brand tie-in.

That's right: the film is just one link in the chain. The arrangement serves the studio well. Above all, it stretches a product's life and opens more sources of revenue, and as competition at the box office grows fiercer, every studio wants both. In 2014 Disney earned more revenue than any other entertainment company and trailed only the retailer Walmart and Apple, yet its studio entertainment division, the film business, brought in just 14% of the total.

Following Disney's lead, every Hollywood studio is trying to become a company that makes and distributes IP. These are not the rules of the traditional film business, but Hollywood has long since absorbed them; the only worry is that it isn't changing fast enough.

The Oscars stand apart from this chain. They still follow, and reward, the traditional way of making movies, in which the point is to produce films. The categories make this plain. The Academy Awards, founded in 1929, honor directors, actors, screenwriters, art directors, cinematographers, editors, composers, sound engineers, costume designers and makeup artists, as well as feature films, animated films and documentaries. Every one of those jobs and categories belongs to the traditional film industry.

And from the 1990s on, the big Hollywood studios spun off their independent-film units as separate companies, whose job was to make the "good movies" that might compete for Oscars, free of any pressure to make money.

To borrow a standard Chinese phrase: the Oscars have become detached from the market and from demand.

For a long stretch of the early film business, though, the Oscars did track the industry's most important changes.

Start with technology. The early Oscars witnessed cinema's move from silent films to sound. *The Broadway Melody*, Best Picture at the second Academy Awards, was the first sound film to use counterpoint between sound and image. Beyond sound, refined design and skillful use of sets and lighting often won films recognition at the Oscars. Most films of that era were crude, and the Oscars set a technical bar for them.

![A still from The Broadway Melody. Image: Douban](/uploads/image/201602/c0723231888a.jpg)

In those days, Oscar prestige and box-office pull also tended to rise together: films the Academy honored rarely did poorly in theaters. *It Happened One Night*, Best Picture in 1935, and *Casablanca*, Best Picture in 1944, earned US$2.5 million and US$3.7 million in their day, very large sums at the time. *Gone with the Wind*, Best Picture in 1940, has grossed more than US$390 million to date, making it one of the most successful films in history.

![A still from Gone with the Wind. Image: Douban](/uploads/image/201602/187c83c45f2f.jpg)

Those films also usually won over the "elite" viewers who, beyond the ordinary ticket buyer, have more say over a film's reputation. *Casablanca* holds a high 8.5 rating on IMDb and ranks 32nd; *Gone with the Wind* and *It Happened One Night* both score 8.1 and rank 153rd and 164th. *12 Angry Men*, at No. 7, and *It's a Wonderful Life*, at No. 25, were both Oscar nominees. Many of the Western films on IMDb's Top 250 have some tie to the Oscars. They were once the mainstream of the market; now people regard them as "classics."

![A still from Casablanca. Image: Douban](/uploads/image/201602/696d47c9292a.jpg)

Today, apart from categories such as visual effects and cinematography, where you can still see technical and artistic progress each year, that healthy link between the Oscars, the market and critical reputation has largely gone. Changes in the Hollywood market explain much of this, and the Academy seems to keep its distance from the market's way of judging films on purpose.

If the aim is to protect the idea of the "good movie," the Oscars may be right. If the films the Academy honored also turned into box-office-crushing IP, well... that would be rather sad.

But as the market and critical reputation drift apart, a "good movie" is no longer easy to define.

For now, the broad judgment of what counts as a "good movie" probably still rests on IMDb's Top 250, the Douban rankings or the picks of certain critics. Either way, the definition is still held by the audience that used to be the mainstream. They keep their understanding of the traditional film market and their demands on film as an art, they control the conversation, and they tell everyone: only films like these are good films.

The market sees it differently. There, a "good movie" is whatever young people approve of. They are more at home with entertainment than with the classic filmmaking of the past, and that taste for entertainment now rules the market.

The capital behind the industry, with its strict demands for returns and market performance, has even changed what the best "good movie" can be, whichever kind of "good movie" you mean.

To secure steady box-office returns, studios now court young audiences the simplest way they can: sequels, adaptations of classic IP and more special effects. Look at the box-office champions of the past two years: *Star Wars 7*, *Furious 7*, *Jurassic World* and, most recently, *Deadpool*. All of them did superbly.

The weight of capital has also brought independent producers under the control of the majors. Big studios such as Fox and Paramount have set up subsidiaries to make independent-style films, and studios such as Disney simply buy successful independent companies to make films for them. Independent producers, remember, have a good record of winning Oscars. *Midnight Cowboy*, an X-rated film, won Best Picture in 1969. David Lynch's *The Elephant Man* and Damien Chazelle's *Whiplash* were both nominated for Best Picture.

On top of that, anyone making films today has to think about a global market, and the center of that market may be China.

What China's film market wants, for now, is spectacle: overwhelming blockbusters stacked with technology. *Avatar* and *Life of Pi*, both technical peaks, fell off IMDb's Top 250 long ago, but on Douban they still rank 93rd and 27th.

At the box office, three of China's ten biggest films of 2015 were Hollywood productions: *Furious 7*, *Avengers: Age of Ultron* and *Jurassic World*, at No. 1, No. 5 and No. 7. No. 2, *Monster Hunt*, No. 4, *Mojin: The Lost Legend*, No. 8, *Jian Bing Man*, and No. 9, *From Vegas to Macau II*, were Chinese films following the same Hollywood formula. *Kung Fu Panda 3*, the recent smash that took 976 million yuan, is an animated film made specifically for the Chinese market.

China's market now claims it will overtake the US's within a few years, and every Hollywood company is doing business with it. New companies such as China Media Capital and Oriental DreamWorks, along with a long run of acquisitions, are slowly bending the world's film production, and the way the world judges films, toward the tastes of today's Chinese consumers.

None of this seems to touch the Oscars. They simply will not give their awards to the market's winners. Never mind that what people follow most about the Oscars now is not the films but the side stories: "Leo," who had spent 20 years as the perennial Best Actor runner-up, and Jennifer Lawrence, the closely watched star Chinese fans call "Big Cousin." That chatter started taking over our social media months ago. Just now, Twitter's trending data showed that the biggest news of the night was not *Spotlight* but Leonardo DiCaprio finally winning his statuette. The second biggest was Jennifer Lawrence not winning hers.

![Jennifer Lawrence, known to Chinese fans as "Big Cousin," at the Oscars. Image: Twitter](/uploads/image/201602/de98c28c32ff.jpg)

Nor do criticisms that sound reasonable move it, such as the charge that the Oscars are too white. Democrats and Black artists make it every year. This year the Black director Spike Lee stayed away from the ceremony in protest, saying the situation was an insult to Black people's dignity and a refusal to recognize their power.

Yet after all these years the Oscars have not changed, and they keep insisting they "have nothing to do with politics." The claim has some basis. The Oscars do not really practice racial discrimination. Black people are underrepresented, but remember that Hollywood is a world Jewish people built, and 38% of Best Director winners in that world have been Jewish.

Yes, the Oscars are a set of rules about film that live in the heads of a group of old people. They do not move with the market, and they ignore criticism that has nothing to do with film. Perhaps there is only one rule: stay detached from the market, and tell us, as people who have seen it all, something the market won't. That is the Oscars' greatest political correctness.

Things may shift a little, though. On January 21, 2016, the board of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences unanimously approved a package of reforms, to be completed by 2020. Its main changes: a more diverse membership, voters who are more active in the film industry, and faster turnover among them.

Finally, the full list of winners:

Best Picture: *Spotlight*

Best Director: Alejandro G. Iñárritu, *The Revenant*

Best Actor: Leonardo DiCaprio, *The Revenant*

Best Actress: Brie Larson, *Room*

Best Supporting Actor: Mark Rylance, *Bridge of Spies*

Best Supporting Actress: Alicia Vikander, *The Danish Girl*

Best Original Screenplay: *Spotlight*

Best Adapted Screenplay: *The Big Short*

Best Foreign Language Film: *Son of Saul*

Best Live Action Short Film: *Stutterer*

Best Animated Feature: *Inside Out*

Best Animated Short Film: *Bear Story*

Best Documentary Feature: *Amy*

Best Documentary Short Subject: *A Girl in the River: The Price of Forgiveness*

Best Film Editing: *Mad Max: Fury Road*

Best Cinematography: *The Revenant*

Best Visual Effects: *Ex Machina*

Best Sound Mixing: *Mad Max: Fury Road*

Best Sound Editing: *Mad Max: Fury Road*

Best Production Design: *Mad Max: Fury Road*

Best Costume Design: *Mad Max: Fury Road*

Best Makeup and Hairstyling: *Mad Max: Fury Road*

Best Original Song: "Writing's On The Wall," *Spectre*

Best Original Score: Ennio Morricone, *The Hateful Eight*
